name: LM5017MRX_NOPB
title: 100 V, 600 mA synchronous step-down and Fly-Buck regulator with constant on-time control
summary: The LM5017 is a step-down regulator for 7.5 V to 100 V inputs with both 100 V power switches built in, rated for 600 mA. Constant on-time control needs no compensation; the on-time follows 1/VIN so the frequency stays nearly constant, adjustable up to 1 MHz. Output is set from 1.225 V up by a divider. It also makes isolated bias rails as a Fly-Buck with a coupled inductor, and comes in SO PowerPAD-8 and WSON-8.

circuits.title: Typical Synchronous Buck Application Circuit
circuits.description: The basic step-down converter for 7.5 V to 100 V input. A divider from VIN sets the UVLO start level, one resistor from VIN to RON sets the on-time and so the frequency, and a capacitor from BST to SW feeds the high-side driver. The inductor runs from SW to the output; the output divider into FB sets VOUT. VCC has its own capacitor to ground.
notes: EP is tied to RTN.

circuits.title: Typical Fly-Buck Application Circuit
circuits.description: The buck converter with its inductor swapped for a coupled inductor, giving a second, isolated output. The primary side is the same as the plain buck: UVLO divider, on-time resistor, bootstrap capacitor, output divider into FB and the VCC capacitor, with the primary output VOUT(PRI) regulated. The secondary winding, rectified by a Schottky diode into its own capacitor, makes VOUT(SEC) on a separate ground.

parts.note: coupled inductor; P1/S1 are the dotted ends of the primary and secondary

notes: GND2 is the isolated secondary ground.
EP is tied to RTN.

circuits.title: Final Schematic for 12.5-V to 95-V Input, and 10-V, 600-mA Output Buck Converter
circuits.description: The worked buck design: 12.5 V to 95 V in, 10 V at up to 600 mA out, near 225 kHz. R3 (499 kΩ) from VIN to RON sets the on-time. R5 and R7 put the UVLO start at about 12.4 V with 2.5 V of hysteresis; TP4 gives access to UVLO for remote shutdown. C4 is the bulk input capacitor and C5 the small one beside the pins. R1 and R6 (7:1) set 10 V at FB. The feedback ripple comes from a Type 3 network: R4 and C6 build a ramp from SW across L1, and C8 couples it into FB. D2 feeds VCC from the 10 V output once that output is up, which cuts the dissipation of the internal VCC regulator; C7 holds VCC and C1 is the bootstrap capacitor. R8 and R2 are 0 Ω resistors in series with L1 and C9.

parts.note: COUT, polarised; X5R or X7R, 16 V or more

notes: The EXP pad joins RTN (pin 1).

circuits.title: Typical Isolated Application Schematic
circuits.description: The worked Fly-Buck design: 20 V to 95 V in, a regulated 10 V primary output VOUT1 and an isolated 9.5 V secondary VOUT2, 300 mA total and 3 W, near 750 kHz. X1 is a 1:1 coupled inductor of 33 µH. The secondary is rectified by D1 into COUT2. RON (130 kΩ) sets the on-time, RUV2 and RUV1 set a 20 V UVLO start with 2.5 V of hysteresis, and RFB2 and RFB1 set 10 V on the primary. Rr and Cr make a ramp from SW across the primary winding and Cac couples it into FB (Type 3 ripple). D2 lets VOUT1 supply VCC. CBYP sits by the IC, CIN is the bulk input capacitor.

parts.note: coupled inductor; P1/S1 are the dotted ends of the primary and secondary; N1 primary, N2 secondary

notes: GND2 is the isolated secondary ground.
EP is tied to RTN.

circuits.title: Low Ripple Output Configuration
circuits.description: A series resistor RC between the regulated node and the output capacitor adds the ripple FB needs when the capacitor ESR is too small. A lower-ripple output is taken straight from the low-ESR COUT. RC slightly degrades load regulation.
notes: Only the SW and FB pins of the IC take part.

circuits.title: UVLO Resistor Setting
circuits.description: A two-resistor divider from VIN to ground with its tap on UVLO (pin 3) sets the input voltage at which switching starts; the internal 20 µA source switched into RUV2 sets the hysteresis.
notes: Only the VIN and UVLO pins of the IC take part.

circuits.title: Type 1: Lowest Cost Configuration
circuits.description: Ripple at FB comes from the output itself: a resistor RC in series with COUT makes the output ripple follow the inductor current, and the divider passes it to FB. RC must exceed 25 mV / ΔIL(MIN) × VOUT / VREF.

circuits.title: Type 2: Reduced Ripple Configuration
circuits.description: As Type 1, with a capacitor Cac across RFB2 so the whole output ripple reaches FB instead of a divided share; RC can then be smaller. Cac is at least 5 / (fsw × (RFB2 || RFB1)) and RC at least 25 mV / ΔIL(MIN).

circuits.title: Type 3: Minimum Ripple Configuration
circuits.description: The ripple is made rather than taken from the output: Rr and Cr across the inductor form a triangle from the SW voltage, and Cac couples it into FB. It does not use the output ripple, which suits outputs that need low ripple. Cr = 3300 pF and Cac = 100 nF; Rr is chosen so RrCr ≤ (VIN(MIN) − VOUT) × TON / 25 mV. The Fly-Buck needs this type.

circuits.title: Soft-Start Circuit
circuits.description: An external soft-start. At power-up C1 is empty, so node B sits near VCC and diode D holds FB above the 1.225 V reference, which keeps the switch off. As C1 charges through R2 and R1, B falls, switching begins and VOUT climbs with FB held at the reference. Once B has fallen to within a diode drop of FB, D turns off and the circuit drops out. R1 keeps B at 0 V afterwards. D1, optional, empties C1 when the input dips so the sequence starts again.

parts.note: example value for the 10 V design, about 2 ms

notes: The values C1 = 1 µF, R2 = 1 kΩ, R1 = 30 kΩ are given for the feedback divider of the 12.5 V to 95 V buck design (RFB2 = 6.98 kΩ, RFB1 = 1 kΩ).

where.RFB2: resistor from the output to FB

operation.text: A 100 V synchronous buck regulator with both N-channel switches inside, for loads up to 600 mA. Control is adaptive constant on-time: the on-time shrinks as VIN rises, so the frequency stays nearly fixed over line and load, and there is no loop compensation. Protection covers input UVLO, peak current limit with a variable forced off-time, thermal shutdown with automatic restart, VCC and gate-drive UVLO, a minimum forced off-time and remote shutdown. The WSON has a 0.8 mm pin pitch and the SO PowerPAD 1.27 mm.

A comparator checks FB against the internal 1.225 V reference. When FB is below it, the high-side switch turns on for one on-time from a one-shot set by RON and VIN. The switch then stays off until FB is below the reference again and the 144 ns minimum off-time has passed. The low-side switch is on whenever the high-side is off. There is no diode emulation, so inductor current can go negative at light load and the converter always runs in continuous conduction.

Regulation works on the ripple at FB, so at least 25 mV of ripple is needed there, falling steadily during the off-time, tracking the inductor current, and larger than any noise on the node. Too little ESR at the output capacitor calls for an added series resistor or one of the ripple networks. When capacitive ripple outweighs resistive ripple, the switching turns erratic: bursts of on-times close together and then a long off-time.

Type 1 and Type 2 take ripple from the output through resistance in series with the output capacitor; Type 2 adds a capacitor across the upper divider resistor so FB sees the full output ripple. Type 3 builds a triangle from SW through Rr and Cr across the inductor and couples it to FB with Cac, which does not use the output ripple and suits low-ripple outputs. A Fly-Buck needs Type 3: with Types 1 and 2 the reflected secondary current upsets the feedback ripple and causes large jitter.

An internal high-voltage linear regulator makes a nominal 7.6 V at VCC straight from VIN (up to 100 V), with internal current limit of 30 mA. It powers the logic and the low-side driver, and through an internal diode recharges the bootstrap capacitor while SW is low. The part starts when VCC passes the 4.5 V VCC UVLO level. At high VIN this regulator dissipates a lot: at 48 V and 7 mA it is 336 mW. Driving VCC from an outside source between 8.55 V and 13 V turns the internal regulator off; an output more than one diode drop above 8.55 V can do this through a diode.

In steady state an on-time starts each time FB drops below 1.225 V. During start-up FB is still low at the end of every on-time, so the next one follows after just the 144 ns forced off-time. A second comparator ends the on-time at once if FB climbs above 1.62 V, as can happen after a sudden step in line or load; the switch stays off until FB is back under 1.225 V.

TON is proportional to RON and inversely proportional to VIN, which keeps the frequency almost constant over the input range. The on-time at the highest VIN should be more than 100 ns, which caps the frequency at high input. At the lowest input the 144 ns forced off-time caps it in the same way.

If buck switch current goes past 1.02 A, that cycle ends at once and an off-timer that cannot be reset starts. Its length rises with VIN and falls as FB rises: with FB at 0 V and VIN at 48 V it is 16 µs, the case of a shorted output or the start of start-up. The long off-time at high VIN keeps a short circuit safe up to 100 V; in a milder overload, with FB above 0 V, the off-time is shorter, which reduces foldback and shortens recovery and start-up. The limit acts on peak current, so the average output current available is below it.

The high-side N-channel switch has a floating driver supplied by an external 0.01 µF ceramic capacitor from BST to SW, which is recharged from VCC through an internal high-voltage diode each off-time while SW sits near 0 V. The 144 ns minimum off-time guarantees that recharge every cycle.

An internal N-channel MOSFET carries the inductor current while the high-side switch is off. With no diode-emulation mode, the regulator stays in continuous conduction even at loads that would otherwise be discontinuous.

UVLO has two levels. Below 0.66 V the part is in a low-current shutdown. Between 0.66 V and 1.225 V it is in standby: the VCC regulator runs but the output is off. Above 1.225 V, once VCC is past its own UVLO level, switching begins. A divider from VIN sets the lowest operating input. Hysteresis comes from an internal 20 µA source that turns on into the divider when the threshold is crossed, pulling UVLO up; the hysteresis equals 20 µA times RUV2. Tied straight to VIN, UVLO lets the part start as soon as VCC UVLO is cleared. Pulling UVLO below 0.66 V from outside shuts the regulator down.

Keep the junction at or below 150 °C in normal use. At about 165 °C the thermal shutdown puts the part into a low-power reset with the buck switch and VCC regulator off; it recovers when the junction cools below about 145 °C (20 °C hysteresis).

An external soft-start circuit uses C1, R1, R2 and diode D. C1 = 1 µF, R2 = 1 kΩ and R1 = 30 kΩ with the 10 V design's divider give roughly 2 ms. R1 should be larger than the feedback divider. C1 stays charged after the first start; D1 can be added to discharge it on a brief input dip.
In typical use the converter steps a higher DC voltage down to a lower one with up to 650 mA available at the output.

12.5 V to 95 V in, 10 V at 600 mA: RFB2 = 6.98 kΩ and RFB1 = 1 kΩ (7:1). Frequency limits work out to 1 MHz at 12.5 V (minimum off-time) and 1.05 MHz at 95 V (100 ns on-time); 225 kHz was picked, giving RON = 493 kΩ, rounded to 499 kΩ. The inductor is sized for ripple of 15 % to 40 % of full load: 40 % at 95 V needs 198 µH, so 220 µH, giving 40 mA to 181 mA of ripple from lowest to highest input and a 690 mA peak, below the 0.7 A minimum limit; it must also carry 1.3 A without saturating. 10 mV of capacitive ripple at 95 V needs 10.1 µF, so 22 µF of X5R or X7R rated 16 V or more. The Type III network uses Cr = 3300 pF and Cac = 100 nF; Rr works out at 57.6 kΩ and 46.4 kΩ was used to leave margin. CVCC = 1 µF and CBST = 0.01 µF. For 0.5 V input ripple CIN must be at least 1.3 µF, so 2.2 µF, 100 V X7R. UVLO at 12 V rising and 2.5 V hysteresis gives 14.53 kΩ and 125 kΩ; the standard 14 kΩ and 127 kΩ give 12.4 V and 2.5 V.

A coupled inductor or flyback-type transformer replaces the buck inductor, and a diode rectifies the secondary. Energy moves to the secondary while the low-side switch conducts. The primary output is usually set so the duty cycle stays under 50 % at the lowest input (VOUT1 < VIN_MIN / 2). With 10 V and 9.5 V outputs a 1:1 ratio is used. RON calculates to 148 kΩ for 750 kHz; 130 kΩ was used to leave room for second-order effects that grow with frequency. The primary ripple must stay under 0.8 A, needing at least 14.9 µH; 33 µH gives 0.36 A at the highest input. A plain buck would need 1.2 µF for 50 mV ripple; the reflected secondary current adds to the primary current in the off-time, so the value is a starting point and 1 µF, 25 V was chosen, with COUT2 equal to it. Cr = 1000 pF and Cac = 0.1 µF; Rr calculates to 66 kΩ and 46.4 kΩ was used. D1 sees N2/N1 × VIN in reverse, so a 100 V Schottky. CBYP = 0.47 µF near the IC and CIN = 2.2 µF bulk (0.5 V ripple needs 0.2 µF), both rated above the highest input. UVLO at 20 V with 2.5 V hysteresis: RUV1 = 8.25 kΩ, RUV2 = 127 kΩ. D2 from VOUT1 to VCC is optional and needs VOUT1 at least one diode drop above 8.55 V.

The supply must meet the absolute maximum and recommended input limits and deliver the full-load input current. Long leads or traces to the supply add inductance that rings with low-ESR ceramic input capacitors and can overshoot VIN when the supply is switched, and resistance that lets VIN sag on load steps. Shortening the supply path and adding an aluminium or tantalum capacitor of about 4.7 µF to 22 µF beside the ceramics damps the resonance. An input EMI filter that is not designed with care can cause instability.

The input loop of CIN, VIN and RTN carries switched current: put the input capacitor right across VIN and RTN (pins 2 and 1) with direct connections; a 0.1 µF or 0.47 µF capacitor at the pins with the bulk capacitance as close as it fits works when all of it cannot be close. CVCC and CBST supply the gate-driver pulses and also belong as close to the IC as possible with short, small loops. The FB trace carries the output voltage and the small ripple the control needs: keep it away from magnetics and from running beside switching traces. SW swings between VIN and ground each cycle; keep its copper small and do not connect it to a plane or pour. The exposed pad goes to RTN and to the ground plane for heat.
